title: Big Walk 4166, 1899 Puzzle Solution
description: On your journey through Big Walk, one of the puzzles that is likely to stump you--and all but guaranteed to stump you if you find it early--is the 4166, 1899 puzzle. You'll spot a box with a puzzle MacGuffin inside of it, and nothing else but a plank with these numbers on it. So what the heck do you do next? Here's how to solve this one. How to do the 4166, 1899 puzzle in Big Walk First, what you need to know is that these are coordinates, if you didn't already surmise that. But coordinates don't help much without a way to read them. For that, I strongly suggest you first complete the red tower. Some exploration spoilers follow from here. 4166, 1899: coordinates to the puzzle answer in Big Walk When you complete the red tower by placing five MacGuffins in its console, you'll unlock a key that you shape and then use to open a room next to the session spawn point, which I took to calling a gym in my time with Big Walk. Inside this newly unlocked room is a massive 3D map on the floor. It's a map of the entire island, complete with locations of every last MacGuffin--and thus puzzle--on the island, as well as other landmarks. While this map is very helpful, it doesn't have coordinates. However, the paper map that spawns on the table inside this room does. It's this paper map that's going to help you find what you need. Open the map and you'll see latitude and longitude plotted along its edges. Recall that you're looking for 4166, 1899. You'll see the rough location of that spot, but if you're having trouble, we've pinpointed it for you in the image below. Head to the red circle we've placed on the map (and forgive the image cropping we've done to avoid spoilers). Then, all you need to do is head there. But remember that at least one person in your group needs to stay with the locked MacGuffin, where you first came upon the coordinates. On your way, you'll probably get distracted by a dozen other things to see and do, but if you stay focused on the task at hand, you'll…

title: 8 Big Walk Tips You Should Know Before You Play
description: Big Walk is one of the best games of 2026. I explain why in my Big Walk review, but if you're reading this, you don't seem to need me to convince you to play it; you're already considering it. Big Walk is an open-world co-op puzzle-adventure with few rules and no quest markers, and part of the fun is in getting lost and exploring the world. I definitely don't want to rob you of that experience. However, since beating the game, I've heard from others who are getting stumped by some aspects of House House's latest project. So I've put together some Big Walk tips meant to iron out some of the details the game doesn't clearly tell you. Focus on one tower at a time… The game begins with a tutorial section of the island. You'll need to solve four puzzles, unlock and shape a key, then use it to lower a footbridge that wraps around a mountain. At that point, you can pretty much go anywhere. What you should do is focus on one of the colored mountaintop towers at a time. There are red, blue, green, and yellow towers. Filling in each tower's console with enough puzzle MacGuffins (my group took to calling them "eggy things") means you'll unlock whatever major item comes with a tower's completion. I won't spoil what each of these towers gives you, but there is arguably a best place to start. For more on that, keep reading. …And the red tower first The order in which you complete these towers is totally up to you, but Big Walk gently nudges you to complete the red tower first, by way of starting you so close to it. It's a good suggestion due to the reward that comes with completing it. It's going to make the rest of the game easier, and though that's true of any tower reward, I'd argue it's most true of the red tower. So start there, fill in five eggy things, and unlock a big prize. Check out these blue structures for helpful items On your travels, you'll notice quite a few buildings that look like this blue one in the image. Inside each one will be either a backpack or a belt,…

title: How To Get Shiny In Big Walk For Big Makeover Achievement/Trophy
description: If you're walking and talking with friends in the land of Big Walk, by now you've likely already customized your characters using the paint studio not far from where the game begins. But did you know there's a second, secret paint studio you'll need to find if you want to access a few special color options and unlock the Big Makeover Achievement or Trophy? Here's what you need to know about how to get shiny in Big Walk. First, you should know that getting shiny isn't required to beat the game. In fact, my group unlocked the true 100% ending before we got shiny. It's totally optional, unless you really want to also 100% the Achievement or Trophy list. Sorry, Switch players. This one doesn't apply to you the same. Still, getting shiny is a fun side attraction and can make your character stand out on your quest to see everything the game has to offer. Given the island can be explored and unlocked in almost any order you choose, I'll provide the optimal path below if you're starting from the meet-up spot where each session begins, but your preferred path might take a different route if you have another starting point in mind. Note: Some minor exploration spoilers are included below. First, you can't access the shiny studio until you've completed the yellow tower. This means bringing five MacGuffins (the little red eggy things you spend the whole game collecting), to the top of the yellow tower, thereby unlocking and shaping the key so you can open the tunnels that run beneath the island. Once you've done that, you'll want to start at the big, red, circular hub where each session begins. I took to calling it a gym or a playground, so I will refer to it as "the gym" from here on out. From the gym, head through the gap to the right of the map room. If you've not yet opened the map room or the shortcut door to the right, it's the one in the image below, but the same goal can be achieved if you just explore and enter any tunnel entrance, since you've at least gotten tunnel…

title: Beast Of Reincarnation’s Cinematic Focus Fails Its Flashy Action
description: When you start a new game in Game Freak’s Beast of Reincarnation, a prompt asks if you’d like to play in cinematic mode. This locks the cutscene frame rate to 24 frames per second, but, understandably, leaves the gameplay as is. When I first saw this during my 90-minute preview session last month, it felt like a bold statement from Game Freak. Pokemon, Game Freak’s multigenerational smash-hit, can be described as many things, but cinematic it certainly is not. Unfortunately, aside from its flashy combat and a few cutscenes, Beast of Reincarnation isn't really cinematic, either. Flat performances and robotic animations undermine its fascinating story, bland environments sour its beautiful art direction, and an overall lack of polish hampers its intense combat. Though there are aspects of Beast of Reincarnation that I adored, for each one of them there’s always something that holds it back. Beast of Reincarnation takes place exactly 2,000 years in the future, in 4026. After civilization was nearly wiped out by a phenomenon called The Blight, an infection that causes humans and animals alike to sprout vegetation, humanity transferred their souls into machines called golems to quell the spread. This inadvertently conquered death, but the relocated souls eventually deteriorated, leaving corrupted golems in their wake. The wildlife didn’t fare much better. Infected beasts called Malefacts wander the ruins of Japan attacking everything and everyone in their path. There’s a captivating history here that weaves together multiple science-fiction subgenres to create an intriguing world. The creatures that wander the wasteland feel biopunk-inspired, the aforementioned golem backstory is pulled from the cyberpunk genre, and the landscapes and architecture would feel at home in solarpunk fiction. Despite its many inspirations, Beast of Reincarnation’s world feels distinct. This, in part, is due to the art direction. The futuristic technology juxtaposed alongside the overgrown…

title: Best Beast Of Reincarnation Skills For The Early Game
description: Throughout Beast of Reincarnation, you'll unlock plenty of skills for Emma and Koo, but in the early game that can be a little overwhelming. You'll first need to decide where to invest your attribute points, as some skills and mods are locked until you upgrade the main skill they're nested beneath. While there are several viable approaches, we think the best way to approach the early game while you're getting to grips with the mechanics is to focus on increasing Emma's AoE damage while leaning on Koo's support abilities. With that in mind, these are the best Beast of Reincarnation skills to focus on unlocking first: Emma's Best Skills Emma's hair is more powerful than it first seems. Hair Emma's hair can be used as a weapon as default, which isn't immediately obvious. However, putting her attribute points into Vitality and then using skill points on the Hair category to enhance it means that enemies hit with her hair will receive more damage. Helm Splitter is the best early game skill. Helm Splitter This skill is nested in the Hair category, and allows Emma to slam down from a height to damage enemies beneath her. You can enhance it, but keep in mind that you'll need to put attribute points into her Vitality stat, otherwise you won't be able to progress it. Helm Splitter is effective against normal enemies and bosses, meaning that Emma can get high away from the danger, and respond with a slam attack. Petal Barrage can target multiple enemies at once. Petal Barrage While in midair, Emma can perform a targeted area attack that deals huge damage. Use this when you're facing bosses, or large groups of enemies, as it'll take down a chunk of their health. Use this time to combine it with an attack from Koo for maximum effect. Tracking Shot Although this is another of Emma's base skills, it's worth having, especially if you use ranged weapons often. Hitting an enemy with her ranged weapon will infuse your arrows with blight, so they'll track enemies. You'll need to have…

title: Beast Of Reincarnation Tips And Beginner’s Guide
description: It can be pretty daunting stepping foot into a challenging RPG. Beast of Reincarnation is deliberately intended to make you approach it like a Soulslike, so there's no shame in admitting you need some help from time to time. Thanks to Emma and Koo's well-populated skill trees and synergies, there are plenty of approaches you can take, and what may seem like a tall order can be made a little simpler by taking your time, reading the in-game tutorials, and optimizing your build. With that in mind, we've put together some essential tips for the early game in Beast of Reincarnation, so that you can progress through the story with a little less friction. But not none at all, because that wouldn't be any fun. Combination attacks have powerful benefits. Unlock skill combinations first Compared to your standard attacks, unlockable skill combinations are far more deadly. Focus on using your skill points to obtain them in the first instance. You'll also unlock some of these as you progress through the story and take down some of the bosses. The first boss, the Rangifier, gives you the Sakura Storm skill. This will unleash a row of Sakura after four consecutive slashes, and you can use them to leap out of the way. Early game skills can change the way you play. Consider where to spend your skill points After you've unlocked some of the combination attacks, focus on what complements your build. The Helm Splitter aerial attack can be acquired early on, and allows Emma to use her hair to get height, and then slam down to the ground for a devastating AoE attack. This helps with both evasion--since you're in the air, some boss attacks can't reach her--and dealing damage that contributes to the stun meter. Menus will tell you more than most games. Read the menus carefully There are a ton of helpful tutorials in the menus, as well as helpful indicators that tell you whether it's worth returning to the cleanse walker. Often, there will be character story beats to catch, or you'll be…

title: Beast Of Reincarnation Difficulty Options – How To Change Difficulty
description: Beast of Reincarnation is the new action-RPG from Pokemon developer Game Freak, and offers a very different experience from the creature-collecting bliss you're used to. It has three difficulty options, with each being designed so that a wider variety of players can enjoy it, unlike a typical Soulslike game. Story Mode is best for those who want to play through the narrative without finding combat too challenging. Parry timing is more forgiving, and enemies deal less damage. You'll still need to engage with the combat, but you'll be punished far less for any mistakes you make. If you're playing this for the Game Freak name rather than a passion for a challenging RPG, opt for Story Mode. Normal Mode is the intended experience, with balanced challenges and normal parry timing. It's intended to encourage you to learn enemy attack patterns, rely on Koo and his abilities, and experiment with your build to find the optimal combinations. Hard Mode is for those Soulslike fanatics who want a serious challenge. The parry window is alarmingly tight, and you'll be punished for any mistakes you make. If you've mastered the combat system and want to experience the game's full brutality, this is the option for oyu. However, director Kota Furushima has explained that the game's challenge isn't just determined by the difficulty you play on. By tinkering with Emma and Koo's skill trees, Spirit Stones that modify combat, and different builds, you can find the game easier or harder as you progress through it. When you're playing, you'll notice that when selecting Koo's Blooming Arts, time slows down to give you the option to think about your approach instead of button mashing and hoping for the best. Make sure to read the skill trees too, as there are many different button combinations for different attacks, and if you're not reading those, you won't be using Emma or Koo to their full potential. Change difficulty in the menu during your playthrough. Can you change difficulty in Beast…

title: 15 Years Ago, Catherine Had Gaming’s Most Complex Trans Representation
description: Catherine celebrated its 15-year anniversary on July 26, 2026. Below, we examine how this game was an early, if awkward, pioneer in trans representation in video games. When Catherine released in 2011 it was a step outside of the box for developer Atlus. The RPG powerhouse team wasn't as popular as it is today, and while it had built up a solid reputation from developing the Shin Megami Tensei and Persona series, Atlus had yet to quite break through into mainstream gaming. When the team decided to develop Catherine, it did so with the mindset of exploring more adult themes and identities. Chief among them was one of gaming’s few examples of trans representation. Though the intention of this character was well meaning, cultural divides caused a bit of controversy in the West. After the long development of Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 4, the team decided to branch out into a wildly unexpected direction for its next title. The project would reunite Persona series director and producer Katsura Hashino, character designer Shigenori Soejima, and composer Shoji Meguro, and take them into an entirely new genre of game that allowed for more mature storytelling. Vincent and Katherine Catherine tells the story of a man named Vincent. Vincent lives a happy life as a bachelor. He has a one-bedroom apartment, goes out drinking with his close friends nearly every night, and has a beautiful girlfriend named Katherine that he’s lagging on marrying. But his life gets upended when he meets the beautiful Catherine, a woman who is temptation made flesh. Soon after their encounter, he is haunted by nightmares every night in his sleep. The gameplay takes the form of controlling Vincent in his day-to-day life, making decisions in his relationships. This feels like a natural progression of Persona’s school and social systems. But the real bulk of the gameplay happens when Vincent goes to sleep and he’s besieged by nightmares that force him to climb an ever-falling tower of blocks in a…

title: Splatoon Raiders Owes A Lot To Older Campaigns You Forgot About
description: Praise for something new can often come at the expense of what came before it. One aspect of art and media criticism that I find irksome is that to uplift new works, older ones from the same lineage are often undersold at best, or completely thrown under the bus at worst. It’s a trend I’ve seen most recently with Splatoon Raiders, the first spin-off title in one of my favorite Nintendo franchises. Splatoon Raiders may very well be the best single-player-focused experience in the series, but let’s not fool ourselves into thinking that the campaigns in Splatoons 1, 2, or 3 were significantly inferior, from either a gameplay or story aspect. In fact, they were pretty damn fresh. The wacky campaign of the first Splatoon isn't to be scoffed at. Conventional wisdom is that the older Splatoon campaigns are the least memorable aspect of their respective games--in short, they’re extended tutorials that are light on story, and Splatoon Raiders is the most successful story campaign in the series. Each of these points might be true to some degree, but that doesn’t stop the story modes of the original three games from being fun in their own respect. Splatoon’s single-player stories are short and sweet, infused with Nintendo’s signature charm. Despite their length, these campaigns greatly expand on the franchise’s world and are dripping with fascinating lore (as well as ink, of course). Many of the levels are amusing ways to learn about a range of Splatoon weapons, with clever level-specific gimmicks for players to wrap their heads around in a way that invokes other Nintendo games. And the structure of these story modes are always changing from game to game, experimenting with the very format of how players move between levels. Unpredictability is the format of Splatoon, and each of these older campaigns fed into the foundation that Splatoon Raiders is built on. The first Splatoon’s Octo Valley campaign did some heavy lifting when it came to fleshing out the Splatoon universe.…

title: We Got Our First Look at Riftbound’s 2027 Release Lineup
description: Riftbound, the League of Legends trading card game (TCG) from Riot Games, just saw the release of its fourth expansion Vendetta on July 31, the first set to achieve release parity among all of the game's available languages. We still have one more expansion to come in 2026, with Radiance dropping October 23, but today's State of the Game update detailed even more products players can get their hands on before year's end. The biannual update also discussed the game's release roadmap for 2027, starting the the sixth set Legacy, launching January 29, which leads into the seventh set Reckoning in April. Sets 8 and 9 details are still under wraps, but the team did tease some details about each expansion's settings and themes. 2027 Release Roadmap Riftbound's 2027 set release dates. The sixth set Legacy releases January 29, 2027 and is the game's largest set to date with 346 cards. It's also designed heavily around the draft format, which makes sense considering its larger-than-average amount of new cards. Legacy also sees the release of a second iteration of Proving Grounds, a collection of four preconstructed decks designed for new players. Compared to the first set (Origins)'s version of Proving Grounds, which had exclusive cards not found in the main set, Proving Grounds Second Edition features cards that can all be found in Legacy booster packs. Legacy brings 12 new playable Legends in to the fold, like Ashe, Garen, Heimerdinger, Illaoi, Karma, Lux, Tryndamere, and Vladimir. On April 30, the seventh set, The Reckoning, comes out. Details on the 264-card set are still minimal, but the update article teases massive Champions and creatures are coming. The Reckoning introduces nine new playable Legends, including Aurelion Sol, Cho'Gath, Shyvana, Vayne, and Zilean. Details for Sets 8 and 9 are virtually nonexistent, but the article confirms that Set 8 focuses on Bandle City, home of the Yordles, while Set 9 teases the importance of the Shadow Isles. title: Halo: Campaign Evolved Reminded Me That Halo Infinite Was Great, Actually
description: Halo: Combat Evolved is 25 years old now, so it's a marvel that playing its most recent remake, Halo: Campaign Evolved, is still as fun as it is. Everything from the weight of the weaponry, the ambiance of the Halo installation, the screams of fleeing grunts, and the grin-inducing sound of a plasma grenade exploding on an unfortunate target are all here to remind you (or introduce you) to the most important franchise in Xbox history. It's a series that has struggled in recent times, and it's easy to see this reminder of Halo's roots as critical to its future. So why do I keep wanting to go back to its flawed, latest entry instead? Halo Infinite was always going to miss the mark in some way. It was a victim of troubled development, responsible for selling a console that struggled out of the gate, and tasked with being both an end to the tired tale from previous entries as well as the start of a wholly new one. Infinite was pitched as Halo's future; a platform that could be built upon for years to come, telling an evolving tale as new chapters were added to it over a decade or more. None of that came to pass. Halo Infinite did a lot of things, but it wasn't enough to pull the series out of the ditch it found itself in. So instead of committing to it long-term, 343 Industries reformed into Halo Studios, shut down its in-house Slipspace engine in favor of the ubiquitous Unreal Engine 5, and did what was once unthinkable: It brought Master Chief to PlayStation. Yet none of that should overshadow just how much Halo Infinite did to drive forward the fundamental gameplay loop that made its original so captivating in 2001. Halo: Combat Evolved has an incredibly strong opening, thrusting you into the chaos of its intergalactic war and wasting no time introducing you to its striking setting on the surface of the Halo installation. Having wide-open areas to explore as enemies drop in from the horizon was as novel then as it is today. It's a little easier to pick apart the…

title: Riftbound’s Card Templates Are Getting A Big Overhaul in 2027
description: Riftbound, Riot Games' League of Legends trading card game (TCG), recently celebrated its one-year anniversary on August 1 during GenCon. Since its launch late last year, the game's undergone dozens of changes, errata, rules updates, and even card bans. In its first of three State of the Game updates this week (and second overall this year), Riot broke down some of the biggest changes coming to Riftbound starting in January of 2027 with the release of the game's sixth set, Legacy. Two State of the Game update articles were released today on Riot's site. One was an in-depth conversation with Riftbound brass Dave Guskin, Chengran Chai, and Nik Davidson, penned by the game's Editor-in-Chief Trick Jarrett, in which they discussed how they felt about the game one year in, and some of the biggest learnings the team has experienced in that time. Regarding banning cards, Riftbound Game Director Dave Guskin explained that the team doesn't set out to ban cards, but will when absolutely necessary, citing the powerful "Miracle" package from Spiritforged. "I don’t regret making powerful things," he said. "We want you all to have cool stuff to experiment with! But as we learn the nuances of making Riftbound (which is something we are doing right alongside you all, our extremely intelligent players) we’ve learned there’s still room to grow in how we approach designing the six domains and gauging the true power of certain game mechanics." Last week's release of Riftbound's fourth set, Vendetta, brought along three preemptive bans in an effort for the team to get ahead of the set's release and ensure it has a healthy competitive meta on day one. The team also confirmed that they will continue to monitor powerful strategies and infinite combos going forward. The other article detailed new products still to come in 2026, and offered a glimpse at the first half of 2027's set releases. What's most interesting from this article is Riot's breakdown of some big changes coming when Legacy…

title: Tongue your friends in Big Hops Together, the froggy platformer's new eight player co-op update, which was inspired by Mario mods
description: Big Hops is the cool 3D platform game with the frog who can use their tongue as a grappling hook. Despite much questing and fervent prayer, I have yet to encounter a frog that can do this in reality. Real-life frogs are a slothful, unimaginative bunch, content to use their tongues purely to catch food with. Some frogs, like the African dwarf frog, don't even have tongues at all. What foul sorcery is here! It's just as well, then, that we have Big Hops, which is being updated with the ability to play through the whole campaign in eight player co-op. With eight frogs in the field, the tactical applications of tongues multiply exponentially. You can tongue items right out of your friend's backpack! You can tether yourself to another frog like in Chained Together, but with the option of letting go before your mate walks you into a laser! The developers, Luckshot Games, are calling the update Big Hops Together. It's available right now in beta, with the official release coming 9th August. Read more

title: Capcom are reworking Dragon’s Dogma 2's infamous Dragonsplague so you can "enjoy the strategic decisions we originally envisioned" for it
description: I know full well that pally RPG Dragon’s Dogma 2 has its Dark Arisen expansion out this year. Still, two years and one megalo-DLC announcement after release, what I still find most fascinating about it is the Dragonsplague: an insidious affliction that quietly infects your mates (or Pawns, whatever) and heightens their fighting prowess, but if left untreated, can induce a bescaled hissy fit that will kill the entire population of your favourite NPC village. Overtuned, ill-communicated bullshit, or laudably bold application of arrogance-punishing friction? These days I lean the latter, but still, what an interesting mechanic that I can think about it on and off since 2024. Capcom, meanwhile, always seemed to play the hedging game, patching in various tweaks and tunings to Dragonsplague in an attempt to placate both camps. The game’s Title Update 3.2, due in late August (ahead of Dark Arisen on October 9th), appears to come down further on the 'Angry fire virus can be fun, actually' side - though according to a Q&A with producer Naoto Oyama and expansion director Kento Kinoshita, these upcoming changes will bring Dragonsplague more in line with Capcom’s original vision for it. title: Fantasy RTS Flow of War is an immediately moreish blend of worker herding, fortress building, and 90s-style visuals
description: My workers in Flow of War are tireless and uncomplaining, labouring away silently in the face of all adversity. Nonetheless, I can feel their seething irritation when I plant my fortress layout awry. Flow of War is a "classic RTS" with an economic element that mostly runs itself. You conjure a bunch of minions from your town hall, pop down templates for cropfields, forges, wells, and suchlike, and watch as your drudges get on with the building and resource-gathering. Where you can contribute is in laying out those structures in an efficient way, so that your serfs accomplish as much as possible before the timer runs down and you have to fend off a fresh wave of attackers, emerging from hellportals around the map. After 30 minutes with the demo, I have mostly learned what not to do. Read more

title: The Soulslike genre has grown stale after Elden Ring, and only FromSoftware can take it to strange new places
description: Sometimes I have to remind myself that I’m a cliché, a person first compelled to write about games because I slew Dark Souls ’ Gwynn, Lord Of Cinder and sat quietly for a moment before thinking to myself, “Hit me, come on, hit me!”. No, I was not okay. But my understanding of games shifted in that tiny university room: they could be overcome, not just completed. FromSoftware’s dark fantasy lands, with their puzzle-box intricacy and dribbly residents, ushered in the "Soulslike" as other developers sought to cash in on masochists like me. Here I am, still a masochist, still someone who adores a Souls and/or ‘like, but who stares at the offerings nowadays and thinks, "Please, someone hit me". These games have stagnated, to the point where it feels like we’re all waiting for FromSoftware to emerge from the fog and beat our asses in a way we’ve not quite seen before. Read more

title: Square Enix responds to Kingdom Hearts Collection AI controversy two months after players called it out
description: Kingdom Hearts publisher and developer, Square Enix, has denied claims that it used AI-generated content to promote the yet-to-be-released Kingdom Hearts Collection 1-3. Fans first accused the company of using AI back in early June, and now - some two months after the initial accusations - Square Enix has responded. Read more
